Description
Hi,
I have multiple custom pytree classes which are inputs to a jit compiled function. When I call the function multiple times and use Nvidia Nsight Systems to profile it with nvtx annotations, I see that the underlying XLA call happens significantly after (even when the function is fully compiled). Here is a screenshot from a report I have.

This is the result of a script like,
nvtx_rng = nvtx.start_range(message="Jacobian", color="green")
J = jvp_scaled_error(custom_pytree, custom_pytree2, ...).block_until_ready()
nvtx.end_range(nvtx_rng)
In my conda environment files for JAX, I have included some extra nvtx annotations for these 2 lines, and added some more in my custom flattening/unflattening operations (smaller yellow regions in above report).
Our custom pytree class is very complicated which has another custom pytrees in its tree definition. I can understand some overhead from flattening and unflattening, but the report shows that actual computation (where we use GPU, it can be seen on the top right with orange(CUDA graph) and blue(CUDA Kernel)) is only one third of the call.
This kind of overhead is not observed in simpler input arguments.
I would like to ask you if this is something that I can omit by changing the registration of my pytree (i.e. adding more static values etc) or adding options to jit decorator?
System info (python version, jaxlib version, accelerator, etc.)
Running on A100 GPU
jax:    0.6.1
jaxlib: 0.6.1
numpy:  2.2.6
python: 3.12.11
nodes.title: `jit` compiled function overhead, help for PyTree registration

Description
When I run the following code I get the error:  TypeError: Value Zero(ShapedArray(float32[1,3])) with type <class 'jax._src.ad_util.Zero'> is not a valid JAX type on the grad_f_x = jax.jacrev(f)(x) line.
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp


def g(x):
    def p(z):
        return jnp.linalg.solve(z.sum()*jnp.eye(3), jnp.array([1., 0., 0.]))[0]

    h = lambda y: jax.jvp(jax.vmap(p), (x,), (y,))[1]

    return h

def f(x):
    return jax.vjp(g(x), jnp.ones_like(x))[1](x)[0]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    x = jnp.array([200.0])
    f_x = f(x)
    print(f"f({x}) = {f_x}")

    grad_f_x = jax.jacrev(f)(x)
    print(f"grad_f({x}) = {grad_f_x}")

I believe the issue is to do with the A in jnp.linalg.solve depending on z. If I move this to the b argument (or remove it), remove the vmap in h or replace h with h = lambda y: jax.vmap(p)(x*y) then the issue disappears. So it has to do with a combination of these elements.
I can also replace p with the following to remove the problem:
def p(z):
    return jax.lax.custom_linear_solve(
              lambda r: (z.sum()*jnp.eye(3)) @ r, 
              jnp.array([1., 0., 0.]),
              lambda mv_fn_, b_: jnp.linalg.solve(mv_fn_(jnp.eye(3)), b_),
              symmetric=True 
          )[0]

nodes.bodyText:
One of the main uses of QR decomposition A=QR is in solving the linear least squares problem Ax=b. In order to solve this problem, the only access we need of Q is the ability to apply it (or its transpose, or adjoint) to vectors, ie we need only blackbox access to Q to its multiplication operators. The QR decomposition algorithm initially forms Q indirectly, as a product of householder transformations, see jax._src.lax.geqrf and jax._src.lax.geqp3 for the pivoted version. This form is efficient for functional access, through the lapack functions ormqr and equivalents, but this functionality is not exposed by jax. Instead, jax exposes only the function householder_product, which wraps the lapack function orgqr and equivalents. Therefore, for the application to linear least squares, we are forced to wastefully materialize the matrix Q explicitly and use the @ operator. This is done, eg in https://github.com/patrick-kidger/lineax/blob/main/lineax/_solver/qr.py .
I believe the best solution is to expose ormqr in the same way as we expose orgqr. This will allow, along with the existing triangular_solve, efficient implementation of the algorithm implemented in lapack function sgels for linear least squares for full rank matrices.
Another remark: It is tempting to expose the functionality of sgels directly (and other lapack drivers) as scipy.linalg.lstsq does. Perhaps this should also be done, but in the context of wanting to do jvp through linear least squares solves, we solve not only Ax=b but systems A^t y = c. Both of these can be done efficiently factoring A only once (this is the approach taken by lineax), but this possibility is not exposed by the scipy.linalg.lstsq interface.
Adding ormgr would also allow an almost completely efficient implementation of sgelsy, which is faster than singular value decomposition for minimum norm least squares for rank deficient problems (allowing one factorization to do the jvp also). Here, to do the maximum, one also wants stzrzf exposed to do the complete orthogonal transformation and make use of upper triangularity. However, due to jax wanting static shapes for intermediate terms (the cannot be rank dependent, eg), maybe what is actually needed is an stzrzf which can be instructed to ignore some zero rows padding the bottom. (I am just starting out in jax, maybe the last sentence is unnecessary for some reason?)

nodes.bodyText:
The function sign(x)*log(abs(x) + 1) is composed of non-differentiable functions, but in fact it is differentiable everywhere.
The derivative wrt x is 0*log(abs(x) + 1) + sign(x)^2 / (abs(x) + 1) = 1 / (abs(x) + 1)
In JAX, it appears that it cannot correctly identify the fact that sign(x)^2  = 1 and instead computes sign(x) twice and multiplies the result. When x = 0, this is wrong. I have attached a minimal example of what I'm talking about. The printed output should be 1, but instead the function returns zero.
import jax

def f(x):
    return jax.numpy.sign(x)*jax.numpy.log(jax.numpy.abs(x) + 1)
        
print(jax.jacfwd(f)(0.0))

Of course, this issue can be solved by defining a custom jvp, but that seems wrong since the root cause is an incorrect calculation.
Perhaps the best way is to do a custom jvp, but I thought I should post here in case there is an easy patch.

Description
The current implementation of jax.numpy.logaddexp2 appears to produce significant numerical errors when using bfloat16/float16 inputs. This seems to stem from how the function is implemented:
@binary_ufunc(identity=-np.inf, reduce=reductions._logsumexp2)
def logaddexp2(x1: ArrayLike, x2: ArrayLike, /) -> Array:
  x1, x2 = promote_args_inexact("logaddexp2", x1, x2)
  ln2 = float(np.log(2))
  return logaddexp(x1 * ln2, x2 * ln2) / ln2

Since bfloat16/float16 has very limited precision, the intermediate scaling with log(2) and division may introduce noticeable numerical error.
Here is a minimal reproducible example that demonstrates the problem:
import numpy as np
import jax.numpy as jnp


def test(dtype):
    x = [-1.40625, -2.32812, -0.769531, -0.71875, -0.851562, -0.878906, -0.417969, -0.527344, 0.921875]
    y = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 3, 0, 2, 4]


    x_np = np.array(x, dtype)
    y_np = np.array(y, dtype)

    x_jnp = jnp.array(x, dtype)
    y_jnp = jnp.array(y, dtype)

    x_jnp_float32 = jnp.array(x, 'float32')
    y_jnp_float32 = jnp.array(y, 'float32')

    np_res = np.logaddexp2(x_np, y_np)
    jnp_res = jnp.logaddexp2(x_jnp, y_jnp)
    jnp_res_float32 = jnp.logaddexp2(x_jnp_float32, y_jnp_float32)


    jnp_error = jnp.linalg.norm(jnp_res - jnp_res_float32)
    np_error = jnp.linalg.norm(np_res - jnp_res_float32)
    
    print(f'{dtype}, jnp error: {jnp_error}')
    print(f'{dtype},  np error: {np_error}')
    print(f'{dtype}, jnp/np error ratio: {jnp_error / np_error}')


test('float16')
test('bfloat16')

Output:
float16, jnp error: 0.001936321030370891
float16,  np error: 0.0016037734458222985
float16, jnp/np error ratio: 1.2073532342910767
bfloat16, jnp error: 0.011528358794748783
bfloat16,  np error: 0.007804871071130037
bfloat16, jnp/np error ratio: 1.4770722389221191

These results show that the error in JAX’s logaddexp2 is ~20% higher than NumPy’s for float16, and ~48% higher for bfloat16, relative to a float32 baseline.
A native logaddexp2 implementation could avoid unnecessary conversions and preserve more precision.

Im timing a piece of code using the timing functionality below:
def mytime(callable, msg='', iterations=30):

	with contexttimer.Timer() as t:

	print(msg, t.elapsed)
	return rs[-1]
The inner loop of the code being profiled looks like this; where k is typically of size [10,128,128]
		# r = jnp.einsum('...k,k', k, unit)   # dummy codepath to isolate the issue to the linalg calls
		try:
			r = jnp.linalg.solve(k, unit)
		except:
			def solve_one_system(a):
				return jnp.linalg.lstsq(a, unit)[0]
			r = jax.vmap(solve_one_system)(k)
Now the strange thing is; when I bump the iteration count in the timing loop above from 30 to 40, the total elapsed time jumps up by about 3 orders of magnitude. This seems exceedingly odd to me; there shouldnt be any interaction between the JAX internals and the iteration count; like there is some kind of memory management problem that triggers upon repeated BLAS calls?

Description
The following is a simple example: with custom jvp rules that doesn't match with the deduced ones, higher order automatic differential rules are generated from the custom jvp procedure. However, the multiplicative rules (including pows) fail to deduce the correct result.
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
@jax.custom_jvp
def foo(x: jax.Array):
    return jnp.ones_like(x)

@foo.defjvp
def foo_jvp(primals: jax.Array, tangents: jax.Array):
    x, = primals
    x_dot, = tangents
    return jnp.ones_like(x), x * x_dot

def fun(x):
    return foo(x) ** 2

x = jnp.array(0.5)
print(x)
print(jax.jacfwd(fun)(x))
print(jax.hessian(fun)(x))
Result: 0.5 1.0 2.0
Expected: 0.5 1.0 2.5
For those unfamiliar with higher-order AD:
Using generalized dual number algebra, namely $R[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^n)$, up to $n-1$ th differential rules (or jets) can be defined. A simple example is where $n=3$, then the algebra can be expressed as the algebra on $x+v\epsilon+\frac{u}{2}\epsilon^2$ with $\epsilon^3=0$. Then taylor-mode AD tells us that $f(x+v\epsilon+\frac{u}{2}\epsilon^2)=f(x)+\partial f(x)[v]\epsilon+\frac{1}{2}(\partial f(x)[u] + \partial^2 f(x)[v,v])\epsilon^2$
With that notation, $foo(x+\epsilon)=1+x\epsilon+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^2$, so $fun(x+\epsilon)$ should be $1+2x\epsilon+\frac{1}{2}(2x^2+2)\epsilon^2$. But jax-deduced result only captures the $2$ part in hessian. Fun fact is that torch-deduced ones (with torch.func) only captures the $2x^2$ part. Thought this might be a general problem so posted here.

#28650 attempted to do this, but it was rolled back in #28690 due to #28671.
Motivation for the change:

Otherwise the default (prepend) mode will add <jax_src_dir>/tests and <jax_src_dir> to the start of sys.path.
This is (has always been) fragile, because <jax_src_dir> has jax/ and jaxlib/ subdirectories, but it recently broke as setuptools 80 has a change in behaviour for editable installations, with the result that if jaxlib is installed editable then import jaxlib with <jax_src_dir> in sys.path will try to import from <jax_src_dir>/jaxlib instead of the editable install location, and fail.
See also:

https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/explanation/pythonpath.html#import-modes
https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/explanation/goodpractices.html#tests-outside-application-code (JAX does not follow the advice here, as there is not a src/ directory alongside tests/ at the top level)

Description
TL;DR: Is there a way to use lax primitives with jit's sharding API?
I'm trying to migrate pmap to jit using sharding arguments. However, lax collectives like psum and pmean seem to fail because they do not recognize axis_name used in those primitives. I'm using flax.nnx, but I observe the same with this JAX-only reproducer:
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp, numpy as np
from jax import lax
from jax.sharding import Mesh, PartitionSpec as P, NamedSharding
from functools import partial

mesh = Mesh(np.asarray(jax.devices()), ('data',))
in_sharding = NamedSharding(mesh, P('data',))
out_sharding = NamedSharding(mesh, P())

@partial(           
    jax.jit,
    in_shardings=in_sharding,   
    out_shardings=out_sharding,       
)
def psum_jit(x):
    return lax.psum(x, 'data') 

# with mesh: (doesn't help)
y = psum_jit(jnp.arange(8, dtype=jnp.float32))
print(y)                
jax.debug.visualize_array_sharding(y)
Output:
  File "/Users/jaketae/Developer/github/jax-playground/src/jit_test.py", line 19, in allreduce_mean
    return lax.psum(x, 'data') 
NameError: unbound axis name: data

I'm not too familar with JAX internals, but the mesh context manager seems to makes axes available via _ThreadResourcesLocalState, whereas lax collectives work with AxisEnv within TracingContext. I haven't quite understood if/how they are related.
Interestingly, using shard_map with jit resolves the issue:
import os, jax, jax.numpy as jnp, numpy as np
from jax import lax, jit
from jax.experimental.shard_map import shard_map
from jax.sharding import Mesh, PartitionSpec as P

mesh = Mesh(np.asarray(jax.devices()), ('data',))

def psum(x):
    return lax.psum(x, axis_name='data')

psum_shard_map = shard_map(
    psum,
    mesh=mesh,
    in_specs=P('data',),  
    out_specs=P()   
)
psum_jit = jit(psum_shard_map) 

y = psum_jit(jnp.arange(8, dtype=jnp.float32))
print(y)        
jax.debug.visualize_array_sharding(y)
Other failed attempts (just jit, no shard_map):

Description
Hello! Out of curiosity, I ran the following benchmark script to compare STFT performance between JAX and PyTorch:
import torch
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from time import perf_counter
from functools import partial

n_samples = 100000

batch_size = 256

torch_device = 'cuda'
n_fft = 2048

torch_window = torch.hann_window(n_fft, device=torch_device)
jax_window = jax.numpy.hanning(n_fft)

def torch_stft(x):
    stft = torch.stft(x, n_fft=n_fft, hop_length=n_fft//2, window=torch_window, center=True, pad_mode='constant', return_complex=True)
    return stft.abs().mean()

def jax_stft(x):
    _, _, stft = jax.scipy.signal.stft(x, window=jax_window, nperseg=n_fft, noverlap=n_fft//2)
    return jnp.abs(stft)

@jax.jit
def jax_stft_vmap(x):
    return jax.vmap(jax_stft)(x).mean()


n_loops = 1000

key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)

key, subkey = jax.random.split(key, 2)
jax_noise = jax.random.uniform(subkey, (batch_size, n_samples))

jax_stft_vmap(jax_noise).block_until_ready()

start = perf_counter()
for _ in range(n_loops):
    jax_stft_vmap(jax_noise)
end = perf_counter()
print(f"JAX STFT: {1000 * (end - start) / n_loops:.4f} ms/it avg")

torch_noise = torch.rand((batch_size, n_samples), device=torch_device)
start = perf_counter()
for _ in range(n_loops):
    torch_stft(torch_noise)
end = perf_counter()
print(f"PyTorch STFT: {1000 * (end - start) / n_loops:.4f} ms/it avg")

nodes.bodyText:
I recently performed some profiling comparing the tridiagonal solvers in jax (jax.lax.linalg.tridiagonal_solve) with  lineax. I observed that the jax call to the cusparse gtsv2 routine on GPU was much faster than the partially unrolled lineax implementation of the Thomas algorithm when unbatched or for small batch sizes. However, if I increase the batch size there is a crossover point at which lineax is faster because jax.lax.linalg scales ~linearly with batch-size and lineax scales sub-linearly/in constant time (and if I manually increase the unroll in lineax to fully unrolled then lineax is faster when any batch size).
I was looking at making a PR in lineax which used the best of both worlds, but then I started to wonder why the jax implementation did not scale as well. It turns out that the jax implementation does not use the cusparse batch implementations (i.e. cusparse<t>gtsv2StridedBatch() and cusparse<t>gtsvInterleavedBatch()). Instead it just performs a for loop over the batch dimensions.
My immediate objective is to get this addressed sooner rather than later to enable clean completion of my lineax PR that I don't need to change at a later date while improving or maintaining current performance. Note my current use case does not include batch solves (I am doing an implicit solve of the 1D heat equation). In the future I may perhaps want to use the batch solve for ADI, multi-group diffusion, or batched simulations.
I would be more than happy to help but I begin to lose track at the Python/C++ barrier when trawling through the source code.
I have worded the issue title in a very general way, if we just want it to refer to tridiagonal solves happy to rename.

import numpy as np
import jax.numpy as jnp

Description
Consider the following snippet.
import numpy as np
def argmax(x):
  @ft.partial(jax.shard_map, in_specs = jax.sharding.PartitionSpec('data', ('model')),
              out_specs = jax.sharding.PartitionSpec('data', ('model')), check_vma=True)
  def argmax_impl(x):
    y = x.argmax(axis=-1, keepdims=1)  
    return y
  return argmax_impl(x)
mesh = jax.sharding.Mesh(np.reshape(jax.devices(), [2,2]), ('data', 'model'))
with jax.sharding.use_mesh(mesh):
  r = argmax(jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(0), (1024, 1024)))
r.shape
Fails with the following message.
98 frames
JaxStackTraceBeforeTransformation: ValueError: Primitive reduce requires varying manual axes to match, but got [frozenset({'model', 'data'}), frozenset()]. Please open an issue at https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/issues and as a temporary workaround pass the check_vma=False argument to `jax.shard_map`

The preceding stack trace is the source of the JAX operation that, once transformed by JAX, triggered the following exception.

The underlying issue appears to be that reduce creates indices aval that doesn't incorporate vma of x.
https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/main/jax/_src/lax/lax.py#L7746

Description
The following numpy function
import numpy as np
np.vectorize(lambda x: x + np.ones(5))(0.5)
returns a numpy array with shape (5,), but the JAX version
import jax.numpy as jnp
jnp.vectorize(lambda x: x + jnp.ones(5))(0.5)
fails with the following exception:
ValueError: output shape (5,) does not match core dimensions () on vectorized function with excluded=frozenset() and signature=None

This is consistent with the JAX and numpy docs (if signature is not provided, inputs and outputs should be scalars), but it might be worth relaxing that constraint to support this use case.

Description
It seems that calls to Array.set do not override or mask previous operations when performing gradient calculations. I am not sure if this is a bug but I certainly found it surprising:
x0 = jax.numpy.zeros(1)

def fn(x):
    y = jax.numpy.zeros_like(x)
    y = y.at[0].set(x[0] - 1)
    return y

print(jax.grad(fn, argnums=0)(x0)) # --> [1.], makes sense

def fn(x):
    y = jax.numpy.zeros_like(x)
    y = y.at[0].set(jax.numpy.sqrt(x[0]))
    y = y.at[0].set(x[0] - 1)
    return y

print(jax.grad(fn, argnums=0)(x0)) # --> [nan], surprising

def fn(x):
    y = jax.numpy.zeros_like(x)
    y = y.at[0].set(jax.numpy.sqrt(x[0]))
    y = jax.numpy.nan_to_num(y,nan=x[0] - 1)
    return y

print(jax.grad(fn, argnums=0)(x0)) # --> [inf], why not nan?
I would have imagined that set implicitly copies the underlying array, cutting all gradient information for the cells being written to, but it seems that this is not the case.

Description
In #28193 I already reported a shard_map bug. I verified on the nightly build that it is indeed fixed by #28197. Nevertheless, there seem to be more bugs for shard_map in JAX 0.6.0. Below is another example for shard_map that works with JAX 0.5.3 but fails with 0.6.0 and also fails on the nightly build after merging #28197.
import os
os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = "--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=2"


import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.sharding import Mesh, NamedSharding
from jax.sharding import PartitionSpec as Pspec
from jax.experimental.shard_map import shard_map

from functools import partial

# prepare sharding
mesh = Mesh(jax.devices(), ("x",))
pspec = Pspec("x")
named_sharding = NamedSharding(mesh, pspec)


# test functions
def f(x):
    return jnp.mean(x**2)
def m(p, t):
    y, fwd = jax.linearize(f, p)
    bwd = jax.linear_transpose(fwd, p)
    return bwd(fwd(t))

# test input
a = jnp.ones((2,))
a = jax.device_put(a, named_sharding)
p = jnp.array([1.])

# partial function
m_partial = partial(m, p)

# sharded function
out_specs = (named_sharding.spec,)
in_specs = (named_sharding.spec,)
m_shard_map = shard_map(
    m_partial, mesh=named_sharding.mesh, in_specs=in_specs, out_specs=out_specs
)

# works for JAX 0.5.3 and fails for 0.6.0
res = m_shard_map(a)





### Similar example to the one above ###

pspec2 = Pspec(None)
named_sharding2 = NamedSharding(mesh, pspec2)
p_device = jax.device_put(p, named_sharding2)
# partial function
m_partial2 = partial(m, p_device)

# sharded function
out_specs = (named_sharding.spec,)
in_specs = (named_sharding.spec,)
m_shard_map2 = shard_map(
    m_partial2, mesh=named_sharding.mesh, in_specs=in_specs, out_specs=out_specs
)

# works for JAX 0.5.3 and fails for 0.6.0
res2 = m_shard_map2(a)

Description
The result of a JIT compiled vectorised function depends on the order of definition of the vectorised function and regular function while this is not the case for the non-JIT compiled vectorised function.
This code example shows that there is a deviation between the result of the mock_fn_vec_jit and mock_fn_vec if there has been a previous JIT compilation of the mock_fn_vec function before. This happens despite the fact that mock_fn_vec_jit is overwritten.
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

# initialise mock input and vmap mock function
vec_input = jnp.array([1,1])
def mock_fn_vec(x):
    return jax.vmap(mock_fn)(x)

# define mock function and jit version of mock function
mock_fn = lambda x: x
mock_fn_vec_jit = jax.jit(mock_fn_vec)

print(mock_fn_vec_jit(vec_input))
print(mock_fn_vec(vec_input))


# overwrite mock function and jit version of mock function
mock_fn = lambda x: -x
mock_fn_vec_jit = jax.jit(mock_fn_vec)

print(mock_fn_vec_jit(vec_input)) # these last lines do not give the same result
print(mock_fn_vec(vec_input))
If one overwrites the mock_fn_vec function after overwriting the mock_fn function, the result of mock_fn_vec_jit is the same as from mock_fn_vec.
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

# initialise mock input and vmap mock function
vec_input = jnp.array([1,1])
def mock_fn_vec(x):
    return jax.vmap(mock_fn)(x)

# define mock function and jit version of mock function
mock_fn = lambda x: x
mock_fn_vec_jit = jax.jit(mock_fn_vec)

print(mock_fn_vec_jit(vec_input))
print(mock_fn_vec(vec_input))

# overwrite mock function and jit version of mock function and overwrite vmap version of mock function
mock_fn = lambda x: -x

def mock_fn_vec(x):
    return jax.vmap(mock_fn)(x)

mock_fn_vec_jit = jax.jit(mock_fn_vec)

print(mock_fn_vec_jit(vec_input)) # these last lines give the same result
print(mock_fn_vec(vec_input))

Description
Running the following script on a Mac M1 I get weird artifacts in jax.scipy.signal.fftconvolve since jax 0.6.0.
I tried to reproduce this on a linux machine and could not.
from functools import partial

import jax
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from jax.scipy.signal import fftconvolve

def build_gaussian_kernel(shape):
    coords = np.meshgrid(*[np.arange(s) - (s - 1) / 2 for s in shape],
                         indexing='ij')
    r2 = sum(c**2 for c in coords)
    kernel = np.exp(-0.5 * r2)
    return kernel / kernel.sum()

kernel_shape = (128, 128)
shape = (3, 256, 256)

arr = np.zeros(shape, dtype=np.float64)
n_points = 200
loc = np.random.randint(shape[1], size=(n_points, 2))
arr[:, loc[ :, 0], loc[:, 1]] = 100.

kernel = build_gaussian_kernel(kernel_shape)
fft_conv = partial(fftconvolve, in2=kernel, mode="same")
convolved_arr = jax.vmap(fft_conv)(arr)[2]

# Plot results
plt.imshow(convolved_arr, norm="log")
plt.title("jax 0.6.0")
plt.colorbar()
plt.show()

Description
Hi,
I am trying to initialize multiprocessing with a simple SLURM cluster, where I have only a single node with 8 H200 GPUs. From the Multi-host and multi-process environments documentation:

When running on GPUs with Slurm and Open MPI, it is assumed that one process is started per GPU, i.e. each process will be assigned only one visible local device.

When passing sbatch options as :
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4
#SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
and running
jax.distributed.initialize()
I get the following error:
RuntimeError: Unable to initialize backend 'cuda': INTERNAL: no supported devices found for platform CUDA (you may need to uninstall the failing plugin package, or set JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu to skip this backend.)

When I update the sbatch like this :
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:4
or like this:
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4
#SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --gpu-bind=closest
and run
jax.distributed.initialize()
print("CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES", os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"])
print("jax.devices()", jax.devices())
print("jax.local_devices()", jax.local_devices())
I get:
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES 0,1,2,3
jax.devices() [CudaDevice(id=0), CudaDevice(id=1), CudaDevice(id=2), CudaDevice(id=3)]
jax.local_devices() [CudaDevice(id=i)]
where i equals the process id for each process. Any idea why this difference?
Most importantly, shouldn't each process see only the GPU on which it will run operations over? What should ideally be my CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set to for each process in a jax multiprocess environment? Is this correct?
Thanks!

Description
The behavior of shard_map has changed from JAX 0.5.3 to 0.6.0. The code snippet below works for JAX 0.5.3 but raises an error for JAX 0.6.0. (Tested on CPU runtime)
import os
os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = "--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=2"


import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.sharding import Mesh, NamedSharding
from jax.sharding import PartitionSpec as Pspec
from jax.experimental.shard_map import shard_map

# prepare sharding
mesh = Mesh(jax.devices(), ("x",))
pspec = Pspec("x")
named_sharding = NamedSharding(mesh, pspec)


# test functions
def f(x):
    return jnp.mean(x**2)
def f_val_grad(x):
    val, grad =  jax.value_and_grad(f)(x)
    return (jnp.atleast_1d(val), jnp.atleast_1d(grad))

# sharded function
out_specs = (named_sharding.spec,named_sharding.spec)
in_specs = (named_sharding.spec,)
f_shard_map = shard_map(
    f_val_grad, mesh=named_sharding.mesh, in_specs=in_specs, out_specs=out_specs
)


# test input
a = jnp.ones((2,))
a = jax.device_put(a, named_sharding)

# works for JAX 0.5.3 and fails for 0.6.0
res = f_shard_map(a)
JAX 0.5.3 gives the expected results while JAX 0.6.0 raises the error ValueError: unexpected JAX type (e.g. shape/dtype) for argument to vjp function: got float32[], but expected float32[]{x} because the corresponding output of the function f had JAX type float32[]{x}

nodes.bodyText:
Dear JAX Team,
We are working on a project that heavily utilizes 1D convolutional and pooling layers across sharded inputs.  We would like to migrate to the new explicit sharding api, but found jax.lax.conv_general_dilated and jax.lax.reduce_window to be breaking for our use-case. Please find below the specific details of the operations with a minimal failing example:
import jax
jax.config.update('jax_num_cpu_devices', 8)  # Run with 8 devices.
import numpy as np
from jax.experimental.shard import reshard


mesh = jax.make_mesh((2, 4), ('x', 'y'), axis_types=(jax.sharding.AxisType.Explicit,)*2)

with jax.sharding.use_mesh(mesh):
  inputs = reshard(np.zeros((16, 128, 7)), jax.sharding.PartitionSpec('x', 'y'))
  # Conv1D across sharded y-axis:
  _ = jax.lax.conv_general_dilated(
      inputs,
      np.zeros((5, 7, 11)),
      window_strides=(1,),
      padding='SAME',
      feature_group_count=1,
      lhs_dilation=(1,),
      rhs_dilation=(1,),
      dimension_numbers=('NWC', 'WIO', 'NWC'),
  )
  
  # Max pooling along sharded y-axis.
  _ = jax.lax.reduce_window(inputs, -np.inf, jax.lax.max, (1,2,1), (1,2,1), 'SAME')

Would it be possible to support this in future releases?
Many thanks!
nodes.title: Request for supporting conv1d and pooling ops with explicit sharding.

import functools as ft

if jax.config.jax_platforms != "cpu":

    jax.config.update("jax_num_cpu_devices", 8)

mesh = jax.make_mesh((4,), ("x",), axis_types=(jax.sharding.AxisType.Explicit,))

sharding = jax.sharding.NamedSharding(mesh, jax.sharding.PartitionSpec("x"))

@ft.partial(jax.jit, in_shardings=sharding)
def f(x):
    x = jnp.expand_dims(x, 1)
    print(jax.typeof(x))
    return jnp.cumsum(x, axis=1)


with jax.sharding.use_mesh(mesh):
    f(reshard(jnp.ones((8,)), sharding))

nodes.bodyText:
Description
When using jax.make_jaxpr, the order of the provided static_argnums changes their ordering in the resulting jaxpr. Consider the following example:
import jax

def f(a, b, c):
    x = a + c
    y = b * c
    z = x - y
    return z
>>> jaxpr = jax.make_jaxpr(f, static_argnums=(0, 1))(1.5, 2.5, 3.5)
>>> jaxpr
{ lambda ; a:f64[]. let
    b:f64[] = add 1.5 a
    c:f64[] = mul 2.5 a
    d:f64[] = sub b c
  in (d,) }
>>> jax.core.eval_jaxpr(jaxpr.jaxpr, jaxpr.consts, 3.5)
[Array(-3.75, dtype=float64, weak_type=True)]
>>>
>>> jaxpr = jax.make_jaxpr(f, static_argnums=(1, 0))(1.5, 2.5, 3.5)
>>> jaxpr
{ lambda ; a:f64[]. let
    b:f64[] = add 2.5 a
    c:f64[] = mul 1.5 a
    d:f64[] = sub b c
  in (d,) }
>>> jax.core.eval_jaxpr(jaxpr.jaxpr, jaxpr.consts, 3.5)
[Array(0.75, dtype=float64, weak_type=True)]
Same is observed with jax.jit as well.

nodes.bodyText:
For example:
In [1]: import numpy as np

In [2]: np.ldexp(np.float16(0.5), 16)
Out[2]: np.float16(32770.0)

In [3]: import jax.numpy as jnp

In [4]: jnp.ldexp(jnp.float16(0.5), 16)
Out[4]: Array(inf, dtype=float16)
This is because jnp.ldexp has a naive implementation which is essentially return x * 2 ** n, which will always overflow if n is too large.
